cloze.text: Extrinsic tongue muscles control the tongue's {{c1::position}}: protrude, retract, elevate, depress.
All extrinsic tongue muscles are innervated by {{c1::CN XII (hypoglossal)}} except the {{c2::palatoglossus}}, which is innervated by CN X (vagus).
The {{c1::genioglossus}} lies in the midline of the tongue and {{c2::protrudes and depresses}} the tongue.
The genioglossus inserts on the tongue and hyoid and originates from the {{c1::genial tubercles}} (inner mandible).
The {{c1::genioglossus}} is the primary tongue protruder; it prevents the tongue from collapsing backward in {{c2::airway obstruction}}.
The {{c1::styloglossus}}, on the side of the tongue, {{c2::retracts and elevates}} the tongue.
The styloglossus inserts on the side of the tongue and originates from the {{c1::styloid process}}.
The hook-shaped {{c1::styloglossus}} pulls the tongue back during {{c2::swallowing}}.
The {{c1::hyoglossus}}, on the side of the tongue, {{c2::depresses}} the tongue.
The hyoglossus inserts on the side of the tongue and originates from the {{c1::hyoid bone}}.
The hyoglossus lies next to the {{c1::lingual nerve}} — relevant in nerve blocks and surgical anatomy.
The {{c1::palatoglossus}} runs from the soft palate to the tongue and {{c2::elevates the back of the tongue}}.
The palatoglossus inserts on the tongue and originates from the {{c1::soft palate}}.
The palatoglossus forms the {{c1::anterior tonsillar pillar}}.
Intrinsic tongue muscles control the tongue's {{c1::shape}}, allowing it to curl, flatten, lengthen, or narrow.
Intrinsic tongue muscles are needed for {{c1::precise speech}}, {{c2::swallowing}}, and fine tongue movements.
All intrinsic tongue muscles are innervated by {{c1::CN XII (hypoglossal)}}.
The {{c1::superior longitudinal}} muscle is the top layer of the tongue and curls the tongue {{c2::upward}}.
The superior longitudinal muscle inserts into tongue tissue and originates from the {{c1::fibrous septum}}.
The {{c1::superior longitudinal}} muscle helps shape the tongue into a {{c2::concave}} form for speech or swallowing.
The {{c1::inferior longitudinal}} muscle, on the underside of the tongue, curls the tongue {{c2::downward}}.
The inferior longitudinal muscle inserts on the underside of the tongue and originates from the {{c1::root of the tongue}}.
The inferior longitudinal muscle works with the {{c1::superior longitudinal}} to move the tongue {{c2::tip}}.
The {{c1::transverse}} intrinsic tongue muscle runs side-to-side and {{c2::narrows and elongates}} the tongue.
The transverse tongue muscle inserts on the lateral borders and originates from the {{c1::median septum}}.
The {{c1::transverse}} intrinsic muscle makes the tongue thin for suction, whistling, or phonetics.
The {{c1::vertical}} intrinsic tongue muscle runs top to bottom and {{c2::flattens and broadens}} the tongue.
The vertical tongue muscle originates from the {{c1::superior surface}} and inserts on the {{c2::underside}} of the tongue.
The {{c1::vertical}} intrinsic muscle flattens the tongue against the {{c2::palate}} during swallowing.
The {{c1::mylohyoid}} forms the floor of the mouth and {{c2::elevates the floor of the mouth and tongue}}.
The mylohyoid inserts on the {{c1::hyoid and midline raphe}} and originates from the {{c2::mylohyoid line}} of the mandible.
The {{c1::geniohyoid}} (midline neck) pulls the hyoid bone {{c2::forward and up}}.
The geniohyoid inserts on the hyoid and originates from the {{c1::genial tubercles}} (inner mandible).
The geniohyoid lies {{c1::deep}} to the mylohyoid and assists in {{c2::swallowing}}.
The {{c1::anterior belly of the digastric}} (under the chin) {{c2::depresses the mandible}} and elevates the hyoid.
The anterior belly of the digastric inserts on the hyoid via a tendon and originates from the {{c1::digastric fossa}} of the mandible.
The anterior belly of the digastric forms the floor of the {{c1::submental triangle}} — relevant for lymph node palpation.
The {{c1::posterior belly of the digastric}} (below the ear) pulls the hyoid {{c2::backward}}.
The posterior belly of the digastric inserts on the hyoid via a tendon and originates from the {{c1::mastoid notch}} of the temporal bone.
The posterior belly of the digastric lies near the {{c1::parotid gland}} and the {{c2::facial nerve}}.
The {{c1::sternohyoid}} (midline neck) {{c2::depresses the hyoid}}; it inserts on the hyoid and originates from the {{c3::sternum}}.
The sternohyoid is a {{c1::superficial infrahyoid}} muscle, visible on thin patients.
The omohyoid inserts on the hyoid and originates from the {{c1::scapula}}.
The {{c1::omohyoid}} runs diagonally and helps stabilize the hyoid during swallowing and speech.
The {{c1::sternocleidomastoid}} rotates the head to the {{c2::opposite}} side and flexes the neck.
The sternocleidomastoid inserts on the {{c1::mastoid process}} and originates from the {{c2::sternum and clavicle}}.
The sternocleidomastoid is palpated during a head turn and is a landmark for {{c1::cervical lymph node}} exams.
The {{c1::trapezius}} (back of the neck and shoulder) {{c2::elevates the shoulder}} and extends the neck.
The trapezius inserts on the {{c1::clavicle and scapula}} and originates from the {{c2::occipital bone and vertebrae}}.
The trapezius (the shrugging muscle) covers the {{c1::posterior triangle}} and is innervated by the {{c2::spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)}}.
The {{c1::scalenus}} (lateral neck) elevates the first and second ribs, assists in neck flexion, and is important for {{c2::deep breathing}}.
The scalenus inserts on the {{c1::first and second ribs}} and originates from the {{c2::cervical vertebrae}}.
The vascular system transports {{c1::blood, oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste}} throughout the body.
The vascular system plays a critical role in {{c1::healing}}, {{c2::immune defense}}, {{c3::temperature control}}, and oral procedures like surgery or anesthesia.
In the head and neck, the vascular system includes major arteries, veins, and a dense network of {{c1::capillaries}}.
{{c1::Arteries}} carry oxygen-rich blood {{c2::away from}} the heart to the body and head.
Arterial blood is {{c1::bright red}} because it is full of oxygen bound to {{c2::hemoglobin}} in red blood cells.
Arterial walls are {{c1::thick and muscular}} to handle the {{c2::high pressure}} from the heart's pumping action.
In the head and neck, {{c1::arteries}} supply oxygen to the brain, facial structures, oral tissues, and teeth.
{{c1::Veins}} carry {{c2::oxygen-poor}} blood {{c3::back to the heart}} after the body has used the oxygen.
Venous blood is {{c1::darker}} because it contains less oxygen and more {{c2::carbon dioxide}} and waste.
Veins have {{c1::thinner}} walls and {{c2::lower}} pressure than arteries.
Many veins contain {{c1::valves}} to keep blood from flowing backward.
cloze.extra: See the Board Alert card on head and neck veins.

cloze.text: Veins are {{c1::more numerous and variable}} than arteries, especially in the head and neck.
In capillaries, {{c1::oxygen and nutrients}} (like glucose) leave the blood and enter the surrounding tissues to feed the cells.
cloze.extra: e.g., oxygen moves from red blood cells into the gingiva so it can stay alive and healthy.

cloze.text: At the capillaries, cells release waste, including {{c1::carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)}}, which the blood carries away to be removed through the {{c2::lungs}}.
Capillaries are found throughout oral tissues, including the {{c1::gingiva}} and the {{c2::periodontal ligament}}.
Capillaries allow {{c1::anesthetic drugs}} to diffuse into nearby nerves and tissues during injections.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::common carotid artery}} is the major blood vessel supplying the head and neck.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The common carotid artery {{c1::bifurcates}} (splits) into the internal and external carotid arteries.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::internal carotid}} artery supplies the {{c2::brain}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::external carotid}} artery supplies the {{c2::face, oral cavity, scalp, and maxillofacial structures}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: Mnemonic for the 8 branches of the external carotid artery: {{c1::FLOSS MAP}}
cloze.extra: Facial, Lingual, Occipital, Superior thyroid, Superficial temporal, Maxillary, Ascending pharyngeal, Posterior auricular.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::facial}} artery supplies the {{c2::lips, nose, and muscles of facial expression}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The facial artery crosses the {{c1::mandible}} near the corner of the mouth and can be punctured during {{c2::extraoral injections or surgery}}.
cloze.extra: It supplies structures often involved in trauma and swelling.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::lingual}} artery supplies the {{c2::tongue, floor of mouth, and sublingual glands}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The lingual artery runs near the {{c1::lingual nerve}} and {{c2::submandibular gland}}; it is at risk during surgeries under the tongue (e.g., frenectomy or sialolith removal).

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::occipital}} artery supplies the {{c2::posterior scalp}} and the {{c3::sternocleidomastoid}} muscle.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The occipital artery is not commonly affected in dental procedures but may be palpated during {{c1::neck exams}} for lymphadenopathy or tension headaches.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::superior thyroid}} artery supplies the {{c2::thyroid gland and larynx}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::superior thyroid}} artery is the {{c2::first}} branch off the external carotid.
cloze.extra: Passes near the infrahyoid muscles — rarely involved in oral procedures.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::superficial temporal}} artery supplies the {{c2::scalp and upper lateral face}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The pulse of the {{c1::superficial temporal}} artery is felt at the {{c2::temple}}.
cloze.extra: May be used in assessing vascular inflammation or trauma.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The anterior branch of the superficial temporal artery lies close to the {{c1::TMJ}} region.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::maxillary}} artery supplies the {{c2::deep face}}: teeth, jaw, nasal cavity, and muscles.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::maxillary}} artery is the most important artery in dentistry.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The maxillary artery gives rise to the {{c1::inferior alveolar}}, {{c2::posterior superior alveolar (PSA)}}, {{c3::infraorbital}}, and {{c4::greater palatine}} arteries.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: There is a risk of {{c1::hematoma}} if the {{c2::PSA}} artery is punctured during local anesthesia.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::ascending pharyngeal}} artery supplies the {{c2::pharynx, soft palate, and meninges}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The ascending pharyngeal artery lies near the {{c1::pharyngeal plexus}}; infections here may spread into the {{c2::retropharyngeal space}}.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::posterior auricular}} artery supplies the {{c2::area behind the ear}}, part of the scalp.

cloze.section: Arteries of the head and neck
cloze.text: The posterior auricular artery lies close to the {{c1::parotid gland and external ear}}; it is part of {{c2::earache}} differentials or post-op swelling checks.
cloze.extra: Not typically involved in dental work.

cloze.text: The {{c1::inferior alveolar}} artery supplies {{c2::all mandibular teeth}}, the chin, and the lower lip.
The inferior alveolar artery enters the {{c1::mandibular foramen}} and runs through the {{c2::mandibular canal}}.
The inferior alveolar artery gives off the {{c1::mental}} and {{c1::incisive}} branches.
The inferior alveolar artery is a landmark for the {{c1::IA block}} and is visible on radiographs near the {{c2::mandibular canal}}.
The {{c1::mental}} artery supplies the {{c2::chin and lower lip}}.
The mental artery exits the {{c1::mental foramen}} near the {{c2::second premolar}}.
The mental artery is a landmark for the {{c1::mental nerve block}} and is palpated during trauma exams.
The {{c1::incisive}} artery supplies the {{c2::mandibular anterior teeth}} (central/lateral incisors, canines).
The incisive artery is a continuation of the {{c1::inferior alveolar}} artery; it stays inside the canal and runs beneath the apices of the {{c2::mandibular incisors}}.
The {{c1::incisive}} artery supplies anterior teeth that are often missed in blocks.
The {{c1::infraorbital}} artery supplies the {{c2::maxillary anterior teeth}}, lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip.
The infraorbital artery travels through the {{c1::infraorbital canal}} and exits via the {{c2::infraorbital foramen}}.
The infraorbital artery gives off the {{c1::anterior superior alveolar}} arteries to supply the maxillary anterior teeth and supporting structures.
The {{c1::posterior superior alveolar (PSA)}} artery supplies the {{c2::maxillary molars}}, buccal gingiva, and part of the {{c3::maxillary sinus}}.
The PSA artery enters the posterior maxilla near the {{c1::tuberosity}}.
The {{c1::anterior superior alveolar (ASA)}} artery supplies the maxillary {{c2::canines and incisors}} and the anterior sinus wall.
The ASA artery is a branch of the {{c1::infraorbital}} artery.
The {{c1::ASA canal}} may appear on radiographs above the apices of the anterior maxillary teeth.
The {{c1::descending palatine}} branch of the maxillary artery includes the {{c2::greater and lesser palatine}} arteries.
Other branches of the {{c1::maxillary}} artery include the deep auricular, middle meningeal, buccal, masseteric, pterygoid, descending palatine, and sphenopalatine arteries.
cloze.extra: The book's chart highlights only the branches most relevant to dental procedures (teeth, palate, surrounding soft tissues).

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::facial}} vein drains the {{c2::superficial face}}: lips, nose, eyes.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The facial vein communicates with deep veins and is a pathway for infection to the {{c1::cavernous sinus}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::maxillary}} vein drains the {{c2::pterygoid venous plexus}} and deep face.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The maxillary vein joins the {{c1::retromandibular}} vein and receives blood from the {{c2::PSA}} area.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::lingual}} vein drains the {{c2::deep tissues of the tongue}}; it is important in tongue surgeries and floor-of-mouth infections.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::retromolar}} vein drains the posterior mandible behind the {{c2::third molars}}; it can contribute to localized bleeding after third molar extractions.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::mental}} vein drains the {{c2::chin and lower lip}} and joins the {{c3::inferior alveolar and facial}} veins.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::sublingual/submental}} veins drain the area beneath the tongue and chin and play a key role in infections that spread to the {{c2::submandibular space}} and beyond.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::pterygoid venous plexus}} surrounds the {{c2::maxillary artery}} and deep facial structures.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The pterygoid venous plexus connects to the facial vein, deep facial vein, and {{c1::ophthalmic}} veins — a possible infection route to the {{c2::brain}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::internal jugular}} vein drains the brain, face, and oral cavity and is the {{c2::main}} venous drainage of the head and neck.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The internal jugular vein runs with the {{c1::carotid artery and vagus nerve}} in the {{c2::carotid sheath}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::external jugular}} vein drains the {{c2::scalp and superficial face}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The external jugular vein crosses over the {{c1::sternocleidomastoid (SCM)}} muscle, is often visible, and drains into the {{c2::subclavian}} vein.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: Veins {{c1::outnumber}} arteries in the head and neck and {{c2::anastomose freely}}, allowing many alternate drainage routes but also rapid spread of infection.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: {{c1::Anastomosis}} means veins are interconnected, so infections from the face or oral cavity can reach deeper structures like the {{c2::brain}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::cavernous sinus}} is located {{c2::posterior to the orbit}}, deep in the cranial cavity.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The cavernous sinus is connected to the {{c1::facial}} vein, the {{c2::ophthalmic}} vein, and the {{c3::pterygoid venous plexus}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The {{c1::pterygoid venous plexus}} is a large, flexible network of veins located behind the {{c2::maxilla}}, near the {{c3::pterygoid muscles}}.

cloze.section: Veins of the head and neck
cloze.text: The pterygoid venous plexus protects vessels like the {{c1::maxillary artery}} from being compressed during {{c2::mastication}}.

basic.back: Tongue muscles that originate outside the tongue and insert into it
Tongue muscles located entirely within the tongue, with no bony attachments

basic.front: Why is the mylohyoid called an "infection tracking line"?
basic.back: It separates the sublingual space (above it) from the submandibular space (below it), so it determines where a floor-of-mouth infection spreads.
Tiny, thin-walled vessels that connect arteries to veins
Interconnected webs of vessels that create multiple drainage paths

basic.front: Board Alert: why are head and neck veins a particular concern for the spread of infection (as many textbooks teach)?
basic.back: They are taught to have no valves, so blood — and infection — can flow in either direction.
basic.extra: Textbooks conflict: modern research shows variable valve presence in head and neck veins, but this has not been widely adopted in textbooks yet.

basic.back: The fluid portion of blood; transports proteins, glucose, electrolytes, hormones, and waste
Blood cells that carry oxygen via hemoglobin
Blood cells that defend against infection and are involved in inflammation and healing
Blood component that helps blood clot after injury or surgery (e.g., post-extraction healing)

basic.front: Why does the PSA block carry a high risk of hematoma?
basic.back: The needle passes near the pterygoid venous plexus (behind the maxilla, near the tuberosity), which is easily punctured.

basic.section: Veins of the head and neck
basic.front: Why is an infection of the upper lip or nose (the "danger triangle") potentially life-threatening?
basic.back: It can spread through the valveless, anastomosing veins (facial vein) to the cavernous sinus and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

mcq.question: Which tongue muscle is NOT innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)?
mcq.explanation: The palatoglossus (anterior tonsillar pillar) is innervated by CN X (vagus). Every other tongue muscle — extrinsic and intrinsic, including the styloglossus that also arises outside the tongue — is supplied by CN XII.

mcq.question: In an unconscious patient, which muscle is primarily responsible for keeping the tongue from collapsing backward into the airway?
mcq.explanation: The genioglossus is the primary protruder of the tongue and prevents it from falling back in airway obstruction. The styloglossus does the opposite — it retracts the tongue.

mcq.question: All of the following are true of the intrinsic tongue muscles EXCEPT:
options: A. They lie entirely within the tongue
B. They change the shape of the tongue
C. They are innervated by CN XII
D. They originate from the genial tubercles
mcq.answer: D. They originate from the genial tubercles
mcq.explanation: Intrinsic muscles have no bony attachments; the genial tubercles are the origin of the extrinsic genioglossus (and the geniohyoid). The other three statements are true.

mcq.question: An abscess on a mandibular molar perforates the lingual cortical plate BELOW the mylohyoid line. Which space will the infection most likely enter first?
mcq.explanation: The mylohyoid (originating on the mylohyoid line) separates the sublingual space above from the submandibular space below, so pus emerging below the line enters the submandibular space. Above the line it would enter the sublingual space.

mcq.question: During an extraoral exam the hygienist asks the patient to turn the head to the LEFT. Which muscle becomes prominent for use as a landmark?
mcq.explanation: The sternocleidomastoid rotates the head to the opposite side, so turning left contracts the RIGHT SCM, which stands out as the landmark for cervical lymph node palpation.

mcq.question: A patient with a markedly low platelet count needs an extraction. Which post-operative problem is most likely?
options: B. Reduced oxygen delivery to the socket
C. Increased risk of viral infection
D. Fluid loss from reduced plasma
mcq.explanation: Platelets help blood clot after injury or surgery, so too few platelets means poor clot formation and prolonged bleeding. Oxygen delivery depends on red blood cells (hemoglobin), not platelets.

mcq.question: Which feature best distinguishes arteries from veins?
options: A. They contain valves to prevent backflow
B. They have thick, muscular walls to withstand high pressure
C. They carry blood back to the heart
D. They are more numerous and variable in the head and neck
mcq.answer: B. They have thick, muscular walls to withstand high pressure
mcq.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure and have thick muscular walls. Valves, return to the heart, and greater number/variability are all features of veins.

mcq.section: Arteries of the head and neck
mcq.question: During removal of a sialolith from the submandibular duct under the tongue, which artery is at greatest risk?
mcq.explanation: The lingual artery runs near the lingual nerve and submandibular gland and is at risk in surgery under the tongue (frenectomy, sialolith removal). The facial artery is the risk in extraoral injections/surgery near the corner of the mouth.

mcq.section: Arteries of the head and neck
mcq.question: Which is the first branch off the external carotid artery?
mcq.explanation: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch; it passes near the infrahyoid muscles to the thyroid gland and larynx. The maxillary is a terminal branch, not the first.

mcq.question: A patient develops a rapidly swelling hematoma after a PSA injection. Which structure was most likely punctured?
mcq.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus lies behind the maxilla near the PSA injection site, making the PSA block the highest hematoma risk. The inferior alveolar artery is near the IA block site in the mandible, not the PSA site.

mcq.question: On a periapical radiograph a thin radiolucent canal is seen ABOVE the apices of the maxillary anterior teeth. It most likely carries which vessel?
mcq.explanation: The ASA canal may appear on radiographs above the apices of anterior maxillary teeth. The incisive artery runs beneath the apices of the MANDIBULAR incisors, inside the mandibular canal.

mcq.section: Veins of the head and neck
mcq.question: A patient has an infected lesion on the side of the nose. Which is the most serious potential complication?
options: C. Infection of the submandibular space
D. Hematoma of the pterygoid plexus
mcq.explanation: The upper lip and nose form the "danger triangle": infection can travel via the facial vein to the cavernous sinus, causing life-threatening cavernous sinus thrombosis. Retropharyngeal spread is linked to the ascending pharyngeal region, not the nose.

mcq.section: Veins of the head and neck
mcq.question: Which structures travel with the internal jugular vein in the carotid sheath?
options: A. Carotid artery and vagus nerve
B. External jugular vein and facial nerve
C. Subclavian artery and phrenic nerve
D. Maxillary artery and lingual nerve
mcq.answer: A. Carotid artery and vagus nerve
mcq.explanation: The internal jugular vein — the main venous drainage of the head and neck — runs with the carotid artery and vagus nerve in the carotid sheath. The external jugular is superficial, crossing over the SCM.
